title: Yunus, Hud and Yusuf
intro: 26 days through three Meccan surahs named after prophets, ending with the story of Yusuf told from beginning to end.

posts.caption: This plan reads three Meccan surahs named after prophets: Yunus (Jonah), Hud and Yusuf (Joseph). Surah Yunus, the tenth, has 109 verses and takes its name from verse 98, which recalls the people of the Prophet Yunus. Here the people of Paradise praise Allah with the words of Al-Fatiha's second verse.

"The abode of peace" translates Dar as-Salam, a name for Paradise. As-Salam, "the Peace", is also one of the names of Allah (59:23), so some commentators read it as the home of the One who is Peace. The verse pairs a call made to everyone with guidance that Allah gives to whom He wills.

This comes after verses about people who hear the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ without really listening. It states a principle the Quran returns to often: Allah does no injustice to anyone, and people wrong only their own souls. "Aught" is Pickthall's old word for "anything".

Addressed to all people, this verse describes the Quran four ways: an exhortation, a healing for the heart, a guidance and a mercy. "Balm" translates shifa, healing, and "that which is in the breasts" is an Arabic way of saying the inner self. Muslims often quote it when they speak of the Quran as a comfort.

posts.display: Lo! verily the friends of Allah are (those) on whom fear (cometh) not, nor do they grieve. Those who believe and keep their duty (to Allah).
posts.caption: "Friends of Allah" translates awliya (singular wali), those who are close to Him and under His protection. The second verse defines them simply: people who believe and have taqwa, a mindful awareness of Allah. "No fear and no grief" is a promise the Quran makes to the faithful many times.

The Prophet Musa (Moses) tells his people to put their trust in Allah, and the few who believed, fearful of Pharaoh, answer with this prayer. Trust here is tawakkul, relying on Allah for the outcome. "Lure" renders fitna, a trial; commentators explain the request as: do not let the oppressors overpower us.

Just before this, verse 98 recalls the people of the Prophet Yunus (Jonah), the one town that believed in time to be spared. Then the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is reminded that faith cannot be forced on anyone. It echoes "There is no compulsion in religion" (2:256).

Surah Hud, the eleventh, is Meccan and has 123 verses. A hadith in al-Tirmidhi's collection reports that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said Hud and similar surahs had turned his hair grey. This verse is gentler: every creature's provision, rizq, depends on Allah, who knows its dwelling and its final resting place.

The Prophet Nuh (Noah) boards the ship as the flood begins, calling on the name of Allah for its sailing and its anchoring. "Its course and its mooring" translates majraha wa mursaha. Some Muslims recite this line when they set out by boat or begin a journey.

The Prophet Hud, after whom the surah is named, was sent to 'Ad, an ancient Arabian people the Quran describes as powerful builders. Rejected and mocked by them, he answers with tawakkul, trust in Allah. Holding a creature "by the forelock" is an Arabic image of complete control: nothing moves outside Allah's power.

Angels come to the Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) in human form. He returns their greeting of peace and hurries to serve them a roasted calf, and his hospitality is often held up as a model in Islamic tradition. They bring good news: a son, Ishaq (Isaac), born to him and his wife in their old age.

The Prophet Shu'ayb (Pickthall spells it Shu'eyb) was sent to Midian, a trading people he urged to give honest weight and measure. Here he calls them back to Allah with a rare divine name, al-Wadud, "the Loving", which appears in the Quran only here and in Surah Al-Buruj (85:14).

Commentators connect the times named here, the two ends of the day and the early hours of the night, with the daily prayers. "Establish worship" is Pickthall's rendering of keeping up the prayer, salah. The second half is one of the Quran's most hopeful lines: good deeds wipe away bad ones.

Surah Hud tells of Nuh (Noah), Hud, Salih, Ibrahim (Abraham), Lut (Lot), Shu'ayb and Musa (Moses). Near its end it explains why: to make firm the heart of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ through years of opposition in Mecca. The next surah, Yusuf, is one long story of its own.

Surah Yusuf, the twelfth, is Meccan and has 111 verses. It is unusual in telling one prophet's story as a single, continuous narrative. Many readers take "the best of narratives" (ahsan al-qasas) to describe the story that follows; some commentators apply it to the Quran's stories as a whole.

The story begins with a dream. The young Yusuf (Joseph) tells his father, the Prophet Ya'qub (Jacob), that he saw eleven stars, the sun and the moon bowing to him. Pickthall's "planets" translates kawkab, a star or planet. Ya'qub senses what it means and warns him not to tell his brothers.

Jealous that their father loves Yusuf (Joseph) and his brother most, the older brothers take him away and throw him into a well. At his lowest moment, Allah inspires him with a promise: one day he will confront them with this deed while they do not recognise him. It comes true many years later.

The brothers bring back the shirt of Yusuf (Joseph) stained with false blood, claiming a wolf ate him. The Prophet Ya'qub (Jacob) does not believe them. His answer is sabrun jamil, "comely patience", often explained as patience without complaint to people, turning to Allah alone for help.

A passing caravan pulls Yusuf (Joseph) out of the well and sells him in Egypt, where a high official, called al-'Aziz in the surah, takes him into his household. There he grows up, and Allah gives him wisdom and knowledge. "The good" translates al-muhsinin, those who do what is beautiful.

The official's wife tries to seduce Yusuf (Joseph). When he refuses, she and other women of the city press him, and he is threatened with prison. He prays that prison is dearer to him than giving in. Allah turns their schemes away from him, and he is jailed for a time though innocent.

In prison, Yusuf (Joseph) explains the dreams of two fellow prisoners and speaks to them of the One God. The one who is freed forgets to mention him, and he stays in prison for some years. Then the king of Egypt has a dream his courtiers cannot read. "Kine" is an old word for cows.

Yusuf (Joseph) reads the king's dream as seven years of plenty followed by seven of famine, and advises storing grain. Cleared of the old accusation, he is put in charge of the storehouses of Egypt. When famine spreads, his brothers come to buy grain from the brother they threw into the well.

Yusuf (Joseph) has kept his younger brother in Egypt by a ruse, and their father, the Prophet Ya'qub (Jacob), weeps until his eyes turn white. Told he will grieve himself to death, he answers with this line. In the next verse he sends his sons back to search, telling them never to despair of Allah's mercy.

On their third visit, Yusuf (Joseph) tells his brothers who he is, and they admit their wrong. "Have no fear" renders la tathrib, "no reproach". According to accounts in the sira, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ quoted these words in 630 CE, when he entered Mecca and pardoned the people who had driven him out.

Yusuf (Joseph) sends his shirt home; laid on his father's face, it restores his sight. The whole family comes to Egypt, and Yusuf welcomes his parents. In the next verse they bow before him in honour, and he says this is the meaning of his dream of old: the eleven stars, the sun and the moon.

Surah Yusuf ends where it began, with the worth of these stories: a lesson for people of understanding, a guidance and a mercy. That closes this walk through Yunus, Hud and Yusuf, from the abode of peace to a family made whole again. Thank you for reading along.
